lines.say: Start a qubit at zero and flip it twice. A perfect simulator says it always reads zero.
But on a real quantum chip, now and then, it reads one. Why?
Think of the whispering game, where every whisper adds a small mistake.
A short line gets the message through. A long line turns it into mush.
Real gates are like whispers, each one slightly imperfect, and a waiting qubit slowly leaks its state.
Before it runs, your circuit is also transpiled, rewritten into the few gates the chip can do.
Two tidy gates can become ten, and each one is another whisper.
Now picture the qubit as an arrow in a globe, pointing straight up for zero.
Here's where the game breaks. Noise doesn't make a new message. It mostly shrinks the arrow toward the centre.
Say each gate has a small chance, lambda, of making the state fully random. So the arrow keeps one minus lambda of its length.
At one percent, ten gates leave about ninety percent, and a hundred leave just over a third.
A shorter arrow is less sure, so the readings drift toward fifty fifty.
Some wobble is just chance. Over a hundred runs, called shots, even a fair fifty fifty rarely gives exactly fifty ones.
A common mix up: error mitigation estimates a better answer from noisy results, but only error correction truly protects the qubit.
So always compare the chip with an ideal simulation of the same circuit.
Every gate adds a little noise. The arrow shrinks, and the results drift toward random.
